content: Boric acid, also known as boracic acid, orthoboric acid, or Acidum Boricum, is a weak acid commonly utilized for various purposes. It serves as an antiseptic, an insecticide, a flame retardant, a moderator in nuclear power plants to regulate the fission rate of uranium, and as a precursor for synthesizing other chemical compounds. It appears as colorless crystals or a white powder and is water-soluble. Its chemical formula is H₃BO₃, sometimes written as B(OH)₃. When found naturally as a mineral, it is referred to as sassolite. Boric acid is primarily produced from borate minerals through a reaction with sulfuric acid. The largest global source of borates is an open-pit mine located in Boron, California, USA. Historically, boric acid was first prepared by Wilhelm Homberg (1652–1715) from borax using mineral acids, and it was named sal sedativum Hombergi (sedative salt of Homberg). Boric acid or its salts have been detected in seawater and are also reported to exist in plants and nearly all fruits. It is soluble in boiling water. When heated above 170°C, it dehydrates to form metaboric acid (HBO₂), a white, cubic crystalline solid that is only slightly water-soluble. Metaboric acid melts at approximately 236°C and further dehydrates above 300°C to form tetraboric acid (H₂B₄O₇), also known as pyroboric acid. Continued heating results in the formation of boron trioxide. Boric acid can refer to any of these compounds. Crystalline boric acid consists of layers of B(OH)₃ molecules held together by hydrogen bonds, with a distance of 318 pm between adjacent layers. The toxicity of boric acid varies depending on the dose. Oral doses of 14 g/kg have been lethal in rats, while doses of 5 to 20 g/kg have caused fatalities in adult humans. According to the Dutch Health Council (1998/19), boric acid is considered to impair fertility in humans and is toxic to unborn infants, potentially affecting the testes in boys. It has also been linked to low birth weight, eye malformations, and nervous system issues. Medicinal Uses: Boric acid is used as an antiseptic for minor burns or cuts and is sometimes included in dressings or salves. It can also be applied as a very dilute solution (e.g., a 5% solution or 1 tablespoon per quart of boiled water) as an eye wash. As an antibacterial agent, it is used to treat acne. Boric acid is effective in treating yeast and fungal infections, such as vaginal candidiasis, by inserting a vaginal suppository containing 600 mg of boric acid daily for 14 days. It is also used to prevent athlete's foot by placing the powder in socks or stockings. In solution form, it can treat certain types of otitis externa (ear infections) in both humans and animals. In the UK, boric acid is used as a preservative in urine sample bottles (red cap). Remarkably, boric acid is the only known acid that is beneficial to the eyes, making it a common ingredient in ophthalmic solutions and commercial eye drops. Insecticidal Uses: Boric acid was first registered as an insecticide in 1948 by the EPA for controlling cockroaches, termites, fire ants, fleas, silverfish, and other insects. It acts as a stomach poison, disrupting the insect's metabolism, and its dry powder form is abrasive to the insect's exoskeleton. It can be used in bait formulations with feed attractants or as a dry powder injected into cracks and crevices. Insects traveling through the boric acid dust pick it up on their legs, ingest it during grooming, and die within three to ten days from starvation and dehydration. Preservative Uses: Boric acid prevents and eliminates wet and dry rot in timber. It can be combined with an ethylene glycol carrier to protect external wood from fungal and insect damage. Borate-impregnated rods are available for insertion into wood via drill holes in areas prone to dampness. Boric acid is also available in gel and injectable paste forms for treating rot-affected wood without replacing the timber. Concentrated borate-based timber treatments can be sprayed or dipped to prevent slime, mycelium, and algae growth, even in marine environments. Numerous manufacturers produce wood preservatives based on boric acid or borate mineral salts. Industrial Uses: In nuclear power plants, boric acid is used to slow the rate of fission by absorbing low-energy (thermal) neutrons. Natural boron contains approximately 20% boron-10, which has a high cross-section for neutron absorption, and 80% boron-11. By adding boric acid to the reactor coolant, the probability of neutron survival is reduced, effectively regulating the fission rate. This method is employed in Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs). Boron is also dissolved in spent fuel pools containing used uranium rods to minimize fission activity. In the jewelry industry, boric acid is combined with denatured alcohol to reduce surface oxidation and firescale formation on metals during annealing and soldering. It is also used in the production of remming mass, a fine silica-containing powder for induction furnace linings and ceramics. Miscellaneous Uses: Borates, including boric acid, have been used since ancient Greek times for cleaning, food preservation, and other purposes. Silly Putty was originally made by adding boric acid to silicone oil. Modern Silly Putty contains elemental silicon, which enhances its bounce by 20%. Lithium borate, the lithium salt of boric acid, is used as a buffer in gel electrophoresis for DNA and RNA analysis. Boric acid is also used in pyrotechnics to prevent amide-forming reactions between aluminum and nitrates. A small amount of boric acid neutralizes alkaline amides that could react with aluminum. Boric acid is popular among fire jugglers and fire spinners, as it produces a deep green flame when dissolved in methanol and burned. It is also used in India and worldwide to dust carrom boards, reducing friction and increasing play speed. Additionally, boric acid is employed in special effects, where its combination with alcohol (usually ethanol) creates a green flame when ignited.
